claim: Communication through body gestures permeates our daily life.
source: Communication through body gestures permeates our daily life.
evidence: This is a general statement about human communication that draws from established understanding of social behavior.

claim: Efficient perception of the message in body gestures reflects one's social cognitive competency.
source: Efficient perception of the message therein reflects one's social cognitive competency.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings and established knowledge about social cognition.

claim: Motion sequences showing agents acting communicatively are perceived to be significantly shorter in duration compared with those acting noncommunicatively.
source: motion sequences showing agents acting communicatively are perceived to be significantly shorter in duration as compared with those acting noncommunicatively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 4.

claim: The strength of the temporal compression effect is negatively correlated with one's autistic-like tendency.
source: The strength of this effect is negatively correlated with one's autistic-like tendency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 showing correlation between PSE and AQ scores.

claim: Intranasal oxytocin administration restores the temporal compression effect in socially less proficient individuals.
source: intranasal oxytocin administration restores the temporal compression effect in socially less proficient individuals
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 5.

claim: The administration of atosiban diminishes the temporal compression effect in socially proficient individuals.
source: the administration of atosiban, a competitive antagonist of oxytocin, diminishes the effect in socially proficient individuals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 6.

claim: Perceived time is highly idiosyncratic and ingrained with one's personality trait.
source: These findings indicate that perceived time, rather than being a faithful representation of physical time, is highly idiosyncratic and ingrained with one's personality trait.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing individual differences in temporal perception.

claim: Oxytocin is involved in mediating time perception of social interaction.
source: they suggest that oxytocin is involved in mediating time perception of social interaction
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiments 5 and 6 showing effects of oxytocin and atosiban.

claim: Mental time deviates, sometimes significantly, from physical time.
source: This seemingly intuitive picture has no bearing on the structure of space-time, yet nicely illustrates the now established finding that mental time deviates, sometimes significantly, from physical time (Eagleman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The deviation between experienced time and physical time has mostly been attributed to sensory properties of external stimuli.
source: To date, the deviation between our experienced time and the physical time has mostly been attributed to sensory properties of the external stimuli (Eagleman, 2008) and their context (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Subjective time is 'warped' by the neural energy involved in representing sensory inputs.
source: It has been proposed that subjective time is 'warped' by the neural energy involved in representing sensory inputs (Eagleman and Pariyadath, 2009; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intense and/or moving stimuli are generally experienced as longer in duration.
source: For instance, intense and/or moving stimuli are generally experienced as longer in duration (Fraisse, 1984) as they evoke stronger perceptual responses in cortical neurons (Mayo and Sommer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intense and/or moving stimuli evoke stronger perceptual responses in cortical neurons.
source: For instance, intense and/or moving stimuli are generally experienced as longer in duration (Fraisse, 1984) as they evoke stronger perceptual responses in cortical neurons (Mayo and Sommer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Most humans efficiently extract others' attitudes and intentions from body gestures portrayed by only a handful of point lights.
source: An important medium of social interaction is body gestures, from which most humans efficiently extract others' attitudes and intentions even when the gestures are portrayed by only a handful of point lights attached to the head and major joints (Johansson, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Human newborns and infants exhibit a predisposition to attend to the motions of biological entities.
source: Such efficacy is considered evolutionarily endowed –– Human newborns and infants exhibit a predisposition to attend to the motions of biological entities (i.e. biological motion)(Fox and McDaniel, 1982; Simion et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The perception of biological motion engages a specific network of distributed neural areas, particularly the superior temporal sulcus (STS).
source: the perception of biological motion engages a specific network of distributed neural areas, particularly the superior temporal sulcus (STS) (Grossman et al., 2005; Grossman and Blake, 2002; Vaina et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) plays an important role in social perception in both monkeys and humans.
source: the superior temporal sulcus (STS) (Grossman et al., 2005; Grossman and Blake, 2002; Vaina et al., 2001) that plays an important role in social perception in both monkeys and humans (Allison et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: People with autism show a deficit of biological motion perception.
source: People with autism characterized by impaired social interaction and communication show both a deficit of biological motion perception (Blake et al., 2003; Klin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: People with autism show abnormalities in the STS.
source: People with autism characterized by impaired social interaction and communication show both a deficit of biological motion perception (Blake et al., 2003; Klin et al., 2009) and abnormalities in the STS (Zilbovicius et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Social proficiency varies widely even among neurotypical individuals and is manifested behaviorally as a stable personality trait.
source: Social proficiency varies widely even among neurotypical individuals, and is manifested behaviorally as a stable personality trait (Digman, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Inter-individual variance in social proficiency has been associated with plasma concentrations of oxytocin.
source: This inter-individual variance has been associated with plasma concentrations of oxytocin, a well-documented prosocial neuropeptide, as well as polymorphisms of its receptor gene OXTR (Andari et al., 2014; Donaldson and Young, 2008; Modahl et al., 1998; Parker et al., 2014; Skuse et al., 2014; Tost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inter-individual variance in social proficiency has been associated with polymorphisms of the oxytocin receptor gene OXTR.
source: This inter-individual variance has been associated with plasma concentrations of oxytocin, a well-documented prosocial neuropeptide, as well as polymorphisms of its receptor gene OXTR (Andari et al., 2014; Donaldson and Young, 2008; Modahl et al., 1998; Parker et al., 2014; Skuse et al., 2014; Tost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intranasally administered oxytocin alters the processing of social stimuli including biological motion in manners that depend on one's social proficiency.
source: Likely through interactions with endogenous oxytocin, intranasally administered oxytocin (Dal Monte et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2016; Lee and Weerts, 2016; Striepens et al., 2013) is found to alter the processing of social stimuli including biological motion in manners that depend on one's social proficiency (Bartz et al., 2011; Kéri and Benedek, 2009) as well as blood oxytocin concentration (Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intranasally administered oxytocin alters the processing of social stimuli in manners that depend on blood oxytocin concentration.
source: Likely through interactions with endogenous oxytocin, intranasally administered oxytocin (Dal Monte et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2016; Lee and Weerts, 2016; Striepens et al., 2013) is found to alter the processing of social stimuli including biological motion in manners that depend on one's social proficiency (Bartz et al., 2011; Kéri and Benedek, 2009) as well as blood oxytocin concentration (Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Social interaction involves two agents acting in a meaningful manner: one agent executes a gesture, the other recognizes it and acts accordingly.
source: In its simplest form, it involves two agents acting in a meaningful manner: one agent executes a gesture, the other recognizes it and acts accordingly.
evidence: This is a conceptual definition based on established understanding of social interaction.

claim: Temporally adjacent actions generally tend to be inferred as a causal sequence and hence communicative.
source: Temporally adjacent actions generally tend to be inferred as a causal sequence and hence communicative (Lagnado and Sloman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Social 'meaning' is derived from the observer's interpretations of the agents' actions and the relationship in between, and is subjective in nature.
source: But ultimately that social 'meaning' is derived from the observer's interpretations of the agents' actions and the relationship in between, and is, to a certain degree, subjective in nature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of social perception.

claim: In Experiment 1, the mean PSE in the upright condition was 69.3 ms, significantly above 0.
source: In the upright condition, the mean PSE was 69.3 ms, significantly above 0 (t23 = 5.60, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.14, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, an upright communicative motion sequence needed to be 69.3 ms longer to be perceived as equal in duration to an upright noncommunicative motion sequence.
source: In other words, an upright communicative motion sequence compressed subjective duration such that it needed to be 69.3 ms longer to be perceived as equal in duration to an upright noncommunicative motion sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PSE data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, the mean PSE in the inverted condition was significantly smaller than in the upright condition.
source: In the inverted condition, by contrast, the mean PSE was significantly smaller (t23 = −5.82, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.19)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, the mean PSE in the inverted condition was not different from 0.
source: In the inverted condition, by contrast, the mean PSE was significantly smaller (t23 = −5.82, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.19) and not different from 0 (t23 = −1.51, p=0.15) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Inversion impairs the perception of biological motion and thereby social interactions mediated by biological motion.
source: Inversion is known to impair the perception of biological motion and thereby social interactions mediated by biological motion, yet does not affect low-level visual features (Troje and Westhoff, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Inversion does not affect low-level visual features.
source: Inversion is known to impair the perception of biological motion and thereby social interactions mediated by biological motion, yet does not affect low-level visual features (Troje and Westhoff, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The temporal compression effect of perceived social interactions could not be due to low-level non-biological visual features.
source: This result hence verified that the temporal compression effect of perceived social interactions could not be due to low-level non-biological visual features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between upright and inverted conditions in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, temporal sensitivities remained unchanged between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: Their temporal sensitivities remained unchanged between the two conditions, as indicated by a comparison of the difference limens (t23 = 0.70, p=0.49).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, the PSEs were not significantly different from 0 when motion sequences were presented upright.
source: The PSEs were not significantly different from 0 regardless of whether the motion sequences were presented upright (t23s = 1.39 and 0.34, ps = 0.18 and 0.74, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 3, the PSEs were not significantly different from 0 when motion sequences were presented upright.
source: The PSEs were not significantly different from 0 regardless of whether the motion sequences were presented upright (t23s = 1.39 and 0.34, ps = 0.18 and 0.74, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, the PSEs were not significantly different from 0 when motion sequences were presented upside down.
source: The PSEs were not significantly different from 0 regardless of whether the motion sequences were presented upright (t23s = 1.39 and 0.34, ps = 0.18 and 0.74, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively) or upside down (t23s = 0.01 and −0.14, ps = 0.99 and 0.89, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 3, the PSEs were not significantly different from 0 when motion sequences were presented upside down.
source: The PSEs were not significantly different from 0 regardless of whether the motion sequences were presented upright (t23s = 1.39 and 0.34, ps = 0.18 and 0.74, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively) or upside down (t23s = 0.01 and −0.14, ps = 0.99 and 0.89, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no significant difference in PSE between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: Between the upright and the inverted conditions, there was no significant difference in PSE (t23s = −1.02 and −0.28, ps = 0.32 and 0.78, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was no significant difference in PSE between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: Between the upright and the inverted conditions, there was no significant difference in PSE (t23s = −1.02 and −0.28, ps = 0.32 and 0.78, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no significant difference in difference limen between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: Between the upright and the inverted conditions, there was no significant difference in PSE (t23s = −1.02 and −0.28, ps = 0.32 and 0.78, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively) or difference limen (t23s = −0.07 and 0.84, ps = 0.95 and 0.41, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was no significant difference in difference limen between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: Between the upright and the inverted conditions, there was no significant difference in PSE (t23s = −1.02 and −0.28, ps = 0.32 and 0.78, for Experiments 2 and 3, respectively) or difference limen (t23s = −0.07 and 0.84, ps = 0.95 and 0.41, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: An omnibus ANOVA of the pooled PSEs across Experiments 1 to 3 confirmed a significant interaction between the vertical orientation of the agents and experiment.
source: Moreover, an omnibus ANOVA of the pooled PSEs across Experiments 1 to 3 confirmed a significant interaction between the vertical orientation of the agents (upright or inverted) and experiment (Experiment 1, 2, or 3) (F2, 69 = 9.98, p<0.001, Cohen's f = 0.54).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: No interaction between vertical orientation and experiment was found with the difference limens across Experiments 1 to 3.
source: No such interaction was found with the difference limens (F2, 69 = 0.23, p=0.80).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The temporal compression effect observed in Experiment 1 was absent in Experiments 2 and 3.
source: We hence concluded that the temporal compression effect observed in Experiment 1 was absent in Experiments 2 and 3.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The mere spatial-temporal correlation between the moves of two agents, without a recognizable communicative intention, was insufficient to affect temporal perception.
source: The mere spatial-temporal correlation between the moves of two agents, without a recognizable communicative intention (disrupted by the temporal and spatial manipulations in Experiments 2 and 3), was insufficient to affect temporal perception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The contingency between the movements of two entities, or the inference of causality, could not account for the temporal compression effect associated with the perception of social interactions.
source: We further verified in a supplementary experiment (24 observers; 12 females) using Michotte-like launching and streaming events (between two objects) (Michotte et al., 1963) that the contingency between the movements of two entities, or the inference of causality, could not account for the temporal compression effect associated with the perception of social interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from a supplementary experiment.

claim: Social communicative ability is a continuum that extends from patients with autism into the neurotypical population.
source: Social communicative ability has been shown to be a continuum that extends from patients with autism into the neurotypical population (Baron-Cohen, 1995; Frith, 1991; Nummenmaa et al., 2012; von dem Hagen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The degree of autistic traits varies substantially even among healthy young adults.
source: The degree of autistic traits (or lack of social proficiency), as measured by the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ), varies substantially even among healthy young adults.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the AQ measure.

claim: Males generally score higher than females on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ).
source: Such variance is particularly pronounced in males, who generally score higher than females on the AQ (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 4, the mean PSE was 38.5 ms, significantly above 0.
source: Overall, Experiment 4 replicated the temporal compression effect observed in Experiment 1. The mean PSE was 38.5 ms, comparable to that of the male observers in Experiment 1 (45.8 ms) and significantly above 0 (t89 = 6.07, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.64, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, there was a significant negative correlation between PSE and AQ score.
source: Critically, inspection of the individual data revealed a significant negative correlation between PSE and AQ score: those with higher AQ scores, namely stronger autistic-like tendencies and lower social proficiencies, were less biased in making duration judgments of the communicative and the noncommunicative motion sequences, and had PSEs closer to 0 (r90 = −0.40, p<0.001, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, the social interaction-induced temporal compression effect was evident in the low AQ group (AQ scores < 20).
source: A median split of the observers by AQ score showed that the social interaction-induced temporal compression effect was evident in the low AQ group (AQ scores < 20, mean PSE = 58.9 ms, significantly above 0; t45 = 7.06, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.04)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, the temporal compression effect barely reached statistical significance in the high AQ group (AQ scores ≥ 20).
source: yet barely reached statistical significance in the high AQ group (AQ scores ≥ 20, mean PSE = 17.1 ms, t43 = 2.00, p=0.052)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, there was a significant group difference in PSE between low AQ and high AQ groups.
source: with a significant group difference in PSE (t88 = 3.51, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.74), but not difference limen (t88 = 0.53, p=0.60) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, there was no significant group difference in difference limen between low AQ and high AQ groups.
source: with a significant group difference in PSE (t88 = 3.51, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.74), but not difference limen (t88 = 0.53, p=0.60) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Autistic traits have been widely associated with reduced levels of oxytocin.
source: Autistic traits have been widely associated with reduced levels of oxytocin (Clark et al., 2013; Green et al., 2001; Modahl et al., 1998; Parker et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Autistic traits can be ameliorated with intranasal oxytocin administration.
source: and can be ameliorated with intranasal oxytocin administration (Anagnostou et al., 2012; Gordon et al., 2013; Guastella et al., 2010; Watanabe et al., 2015; Yatawara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Atosiban is a desamino-oxytocin analogue and a competitive oxytocin receptor antagonist.
source: Atosiban is a desamino-oxytocin analogue and a competitive oxytocin receptor antagonist (Sanu and Lamont, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Atosiban is centrally available when administered intranasally.
source: and has been shown to be centrally available when administered intranasally (Lamont and Kam, 2008; Lundin et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 5, in those treated with oxytocin, the mean PSE significantly increased by 36.9 ms.
source: In those treated with oxytocin, the mean PSE significantly increased by 36.9 ms (t39 = 3.68, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.58)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, the baseline mean PSE for the oxytocin group was 13.3 ms, which was not significantly different from 0.
source: from 13.3 ms at baseline, which was not significantly different from 0 (t39 = 1.34, p=0.19)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, the mean PSE after oxytocin administration was 50.1 ms, significantly above 0.
source: to 50.1 ms after oxytocin administration (significantly above 0, t39 = 4.22, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.66) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, in those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE was not significantly different from 0 at baseline.
source: By contrast, in those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE was not significantly different from 0 both at baseline (9.7 ms, t39 = 1.14, p=0.26)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, in those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE was not significantly different from 0 after atosiban administration.
source: and after atosiban administration (−9.4 ms, t39 = −1.11, p=0.28)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, in those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE showed a significant reduction.
source: yet numerically showed a significant reduction (t39 = −2.24, p=0.031, Cohen's d = −0.35) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, there was a marked difference in the changes in PSEs pre- and post-drug administration between the oxytocin and atosiban groups.
source: Between the two drug groups, there was a marked difference in the changes in PSEs pre- and post- drug administration (t78 = 4.25, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.95).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, the difference limens remained unaltered before and after drug administration for both oxytocin and atosiban groups.
source: These effects could not be due to changes of the observers' temporal sensitivity, as their difference limens remained unaltered before and after drug administration (t39s = 0.35 and −0.66, ps = 0.73 and 0.51, for oxytocin and atosiban, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 5, transient mood states were unaffected by drug condition.
source: Besides, their transient mood states, as reflected by ratings on the Profile of Mood States (POMS) scale (McNair et al., 1971), were also unaffected by drug condition (drug condition ×testing session; total mood disturbance: F1, 78 = 0.18, p=0.68; all subscales: ps > 0.1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, at baseline, the observers in both drug groups were significantly biased towards perceiving the communicative motion sequences as shorter in duration than the noncommunicative ones.
source: At baseline, the observers in both drug groups were significantly biased towards perceiving the communicative motion sequences as shorter in duration than the noncommunicative ones (mean PSEs = 48.6 ms and 54.5 ms, t39s = 4.32 and 5.94, ps < 0.001, Cohen's ds = 0.68 and 0.94, for atosiban and saline, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, at baseline, there was no difference in PSE between the atosiban and saline groups.
source: with no difference in between (t78 = 0.41, p=0.68) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, after drug treatments, a significant group difference in PSE emerged between the atosiban and saline groups.
source: After drug treatments, however, a significant group difference emerged (mean PSEs = 17.5 ms and 46.8 ms, t78 = 2.64, p=0.010, Cohen's d = 0.59).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, in those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE dropped significantly by 31.1 ms.
source: In those treated with atosiban, the mean PSE dropped significantly by 31.1 ms (t39 = −3.90, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −0.62)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, after atosiban treatment, the mean PSE was still significantly above 0.
source: albeit still significantly above 0 (t39 = 2.04, p=0.048, Cohen's d = 0.32) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, in those treated with saline, the PSEs were unaffected.
source: By contrast, in those treated with saline, the PSEs were unaffected (t39 = −1.13, p=0.26; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, there was a significant difference between the atosiban and saline groups in the changes in PSEs pre- and post-drug administration.
source: There was a significant difference between the two drug groups in the changes in PSEs pre- and post- drug administration (t78 = 2.22, p=0.029, Cohen's d = 0.50).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, the difference limens in both groups remained unchanged.
source: Meanwhile, the difference limens in both groups remained unchanged (t39s = −1.07 and −1.11, ps = 0.29 and 0.27, for atosiban and saline, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 6, the POMS ratings were unaffected by drug condition.
source: and the POMS ratings were unaffected by drug condition (drug condition ×testing session; total mood disturbance: F1, 78 = 0.47, p=0.50; all subscales: ps > 0.2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Distortion of time perception has been widely associated with properties of the stimuli.
source: Whereas distortion of time perception has been widely associated with properties of the stimuli (Eagleman, 2008) and the context (Shi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings provide the first empirical evidence that links the subjective time of an event with a personality trait, namely social proficiency.
source: these findings provide, to our best knowledge, the first empirical evidence that links the subjective time of an event with a personality trait, namely social proficiency.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Social perception involves multifaceted information processing that culminates in the accurate recognition of others' dispositions and intensions.
source: Social perception involves multifaceted information processing that culminates in the accurate recognition of others' dispositions and intensions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about social perception.

claim: Social perception inherently entails the integration of information, including causal integration and cognitive algebra.
source: It inherently entails the integration of information, including the integration between origin and effect (causal integration), the integration of clues (e.g. motion cues) to form impressions, extract intentions, and arrive at judgments (cognitive algebra), etc (Anderson, 1981; Blythe et al., 1999; Heider, 1944; Smith, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Autism spectrum disorders have been associated with deficits in sensory integration.
source: Autism spectrum disorders have been associated with deficits in sensory integration (Brandwein et al., 2013; Gepner and Mestre, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Autism spectrum disorders are not associated with deficits in unisensory temporal function per se.
source: though not with unisensory temporal function per se (Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Deficits in sensory integration may cascade into the domain of social interactions and partially cause the observed effects.
source: It is plausible that such deficits cascade into the domain of social interactions and partially cause the aforementioned effects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism underlying the findings.

claim: Multiple brain regions are engaged in social perception, including the STS, TPJ, and dmPFC.
source: Multiple brain regions are engaged in social perception, and coordinately enable efficient assessment and interpretation of social signals. They include not only the STS that supports the understanding of actions (Allison et al., 2000), but also higher cortical areas like the temporal-parietal junction (TPJ) that represents mental states (Carter and Huettel, 2013) and the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) that is implicated in the uniquely human representation of triadic interactions between two minds and an object (Saxe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction (TPJ) represents mental states.
source: but also higher cortical areas like the temporal-parietal junction (TPJ) that represents mental states (Carter and Huettel, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) is implicated in the uniquely human representation of triadic interactions between two minds and an object.
source: and the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) that is implicated in the uniquely human representation of triadic interactions between two minds and an object (Saxe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The observed temporal compression effect likely arises from higher stages of social processing.
source: The observed temporal compression effect, being independent of the perception of biological motion, likely arises from these higher stages of social processing (Cusack et al., 2015; von der Lühe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to prior research.

claim: Subjective time has been proposed to be a signature of the amount of energy expended in representing a stimulus.
source: Subjective time has been proposed to be a signature of the amount of energy expended in representing a stimulus (Eagleman and Pariyadath, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Communicative motion sequences are processed with increased efficiency in TPJ and dmPFC relative to motion sequences without a recognizable communicative intention, leading to lowered metabolic cost and shortened subjective duration.
source: It is plausible that communicative motion sequences are processed with increased efficiency in TPJ and dmPFC relative to motion sequences without a recognizable communicative intention, thus leading to lowered metabolic cost (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008; Laughlin, 2001) and shortened subjective duration, particularly in socially proficient individuals.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism, supported by citations to prior research on metabolic cost.

claim: The temporal compression effect cannot be accounted for by the operation of a dedicated neural module specialized for representing the temporal relationships between events.
source: Of note here is that this temporal compression effect can hardly be accounted for by the operation of a dedicated neural module specialized for representing the temporal relationships between events (Ivry and Schlerf, 2008), since it is specific to the perception of social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the effect to social interactions.

claim: Oxytocin partially drives social motivation.
source: Oxytocin partially drives social motivation (Dölen et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Oxytocin has been identified as an important modulator of social behaviors ranging from social recognition to consolation and ethnocentrism.
source: and has increasingly been identified as an important modulator of social behaviors (Carter, 2014; Donaldson and Young, 2008) ranging from social recognition (Oettl et al., 2016) to consolation (Burkett et al., 2016) and ethnocentrism (De Dreu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oxytocin has been linked to repetitive behaviors, a core feature of autism.
source: It has also been linked to repetitive behaviors –– a core feature of autism (Hollander et al., 2003; Insel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The application of oxytocin modulates responses in the STS, TPJ and the prefrontal cortex in various social cognitive tasks.
source: Results from human brain imaging studies indicate that the application of oxytocin modulates responses in the STS, TPJ and the prefrontal cortex, among others, in various social cognitive tasks (Zink and Meyer-Lindenberg, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Alterations of neural activities by oxytocin presumably facilitate social processing in socially less proficient individuals.
source: Such alterations of neural activities presumably facilitate social processing in socially less proficient individuals, where exogenous oxytocin has been shown to exert a more definitive prosocial effect (Bartz et al., 2010; Bartz et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research showing prosocial effects of oxytocin.

claim: Exogenous oxytocin has been shown to exert a more definitive prosocial effect in socially less proficient individuals.
source: where exogenous oxytocin has been shown to exert a more definitive prosocial effect (Bartz et al., 2010; Bartz et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In socially proficient individuals, the influence of exogenous oxytocin is more complicated and hard to predict and interpret.
source: In socially proficient individuals, the influence of exogenous oxytocin is more complicated, even hard to predict and interpret (Bartz, 2016; Bartz et al., 2010; Bartz et al., 2011; Olff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The comparison between oxytocin and atosiban spoke directly to the role of oxytocin in mediating time perception of social interactions.
source: The comparison between oxytocin and atosiban spoke directly to the role of oxytocin in mediating time perception of social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design and results.

claim: Pharmacological research on time perception has primarily focused on dopamine, serotonin and acetylcholine.
source: This finding also adds to and extends the extant pharmacological research on time perception, which has primarily focused on dopamine, serotonin and acetylcholine (Allman and Meck, 2012; Meck, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The perceived duration of social interactions is a product of complex neuroendocrine and neural processes.
source: We conclude that the perceived duration of social interactions is a product of complex neuroendocrine and neural processes, the exact mechanism awaiting further investigation, and is ingrained with one's social traits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Subjective time is not only nonuniform but also idiosyncratic.
source: Subjective time is not only nonuniform, like Einstein alluded to in his analogy, but also idiosyncratic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: In Experiment 1, 24 observers (12 females) performed the duration judgment task.
source: Twenty-four observers (12 females) performed the duration judgment task in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: Sample sizes in Experiments 1-3 were determined by G*Power to be sufficient to detect a large temporal distortion effect in time perception (d ≥ 0.8), at a power larger than 95%.
source: Sample sizes were determined by G*Power to be sufficient to detect a large temporal distortion effect in time perception (d ≥ 0.8), at a power larger than 95%.
evidence: This describes the power analysis used to determine sample size.

claim: The effect size for sample size determination was estimated based on an earlier study that employed biological motion stimuli and similar psychophysical testing procedures.
source: The effect size was estimated based on an earlier study that employed biological motion stimuli and similar psychophysical testing procedures to those in the current study (Wang and Jiang, 2012).
evidence: This describes the basis for the effect size estimate, supported by citation.

claim: In Experiment 4, 90 males participated.
source: An independent group of 90 males (22.5 ± 2.7 years) took part in Experiment 4.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: In Experiment 5, 80 male non-smokers who scored above or equal to 20 on the AQ participated.
source: In addition, 80 male non-smokers (22.1 ± 2.6 years) who scored above or equal to 20 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) (mean AQ score ±SD = 24.9±4.3) participated in Experiment 5.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: In Experiment 6, 80 male non-smokers with AQ scores below 20 participated.
source: Another 80 male non-smokers (22.8 ± 2.3 years) with AQ scores below 20 (15.5 ± 2.7) participated in Experiment 6.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: Only males were recruited in Experiments 4-6 to take advantage of men's pronounced variance in social proficiency.
source: Only males were recruited in Experiments 4–6 for the following reasons: In Experiment 4, this was done to take advantage of men's pronounced variance in social proficiency (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the sample selection, supported by citation.

claim: Only males were recruited in Experiments 5 and 6 because oxytocin and atosiban respectively cause and antagonize contractions of the uterus.
source: In Experiments 5 and 6, this was due to pragmatic reasons (like most intranasal oxytocin studies), as oxytocin and atosiban respectively cause and antagonize contractions of the uterus.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the sample selection based on physiological considerations.

claim: Ten communicative point-light motion sequences were chosen from the Communicative Interaction Database, each portraying two agents of the same gender engaging in either a dyadic or triadic interaction.
source: Ten communicative point-light motion sequences (C1-10 in Supplementary file 1), each portraying two agents of the same gender engaging in either a face-to-face (dyadic, two motion sequences) or a person-object-person (triadic, eight motion sequences) interaction, were chosen from the Communicative Interaction Database (Manera et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the stimulus selection, supported by citation.

claim: Noncommunicative motion sequences were produced by cross-pairing the agents of the same gender from different interactions.
source: By cross-pairing the agents of the same gender from different interactions, we produced an essentially physically matched set of 10 noncommunicative motion sequences (NC1-10 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the method for creating control stimuli.

claim: The noncommunicative motion sequences were perceived as significantly less communicative than the communicative ones.
source: We verified in an independent group of 24 observers (half male, 27.5 ± 3.3 years) that the noncommunicative motion sequences were perceived as significantly less communicative than the communicative ones (normalized communicativeness rating: 0.37 vs. 0.71, t23 = −8.11, p<0.0001, Cohen's d = −1.66).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from a validation study.

claim: In Experiment 2, a temporal lag of 700 ms was introduced in between every two acting agents.
source: Specifically, we introduced a temporal lag of 700 ms (21 frames) in between every two acting agents (communicative and noncommunicative, upright and inverted) in Experiment 2 (Manera et al., 2013)
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation, supported by citation.

claim: In Experiment 3, the two agents in each display were spatially swapped such that they faced in opposite directions instead of facing each other.
source: and spatially swapped the two agents in each display in Experiment 3 such that they faced in opposite directions instead of facing each other.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: In each trial of the duration judgment task, observers were shown two motion sequences sequentially and asked to report which appeared longer in duration.
source: Each trial of the duration judgment task in Experiment 1 began with a fixation on a central cross (1°×1°) for 1000 ms, followed by two sequentially presented motion sequences –– one communicative, the other noncommunicative, in random order with a blank screen of 400–600 ms in between (Figure 1). One of the motion sequences (communicative or noncommunicative, each in half of the trials in random order) was presented for 1000 ms, the other for 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400 or 1600 ms with equal possibility. That is, the duration difference between the communicative and the noncommunicative motion sequences ranged from −600 ms to 600 ms in steps of 200 ms. Observers were asked to press one of two buttons to indicate which motion sequence (the first or the second) was longer in duration
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The duration judgment task did not require recognitions of the nature of the motion sequences.
source: a task that did not require recognitions of the nature of the motion sequences.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental task.

claim: In Experiment 5, observers self-administered a single intranasal dose of 24 IU of oxytocin or 60 µg of atosiban.
source: Observers in Experiments 5 and 6 self-administered a single intranasal dose of 24 IU of oxytocin (ProSpec,>99.0% as determined by RP-HPLC, dissolved in saline; three puffs per nostril, each with 4 IU of oxytocin; for half of the observers in Experiment 5), 60 µg of atosiban (ProSpec,>99.0% as determined by RP-HPLC, dissolved in saline; three puffs per nostril, each with 10 µg of atosiban; for half of the observers in Experiments 5 and 6)
evidence: This describes the drug administration procedure.

claim: In Experiment 6, observers self-administered either 60 µg of atosiban or saline.
source: 60 µg of atosiban (ProSpec,>99.0% as determined by RP-HPLC, dissolved in saline; three puffs per nostril, each with 10 µg of atosiban; for half of the observers in Experiments 5 and 6) or saline (three puffs per nostril, for half of the observers in Experiment 6)
evidence: This describes the drug administration procedure.

claim: Drug administration in Experiments 5 and 6 was done in a randomized between-subjects manner.
source: in a randomized between-subjects manner, after they completed the baseline blocks of the duration judgment task and the Profile of Mood States scale.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Neither the participants nor the experimenters were aware of the identity of the drug used in Experiments 5 and 6.
source: Neither the participants nor the experimenters were aware of the identity of the drug used.
evidence: This describes the blinding procedure.

claim: Both oxytocin and atosiban have been shown to be bioavailable when administered intranasally.
source: Both oxytocin (Dal Monte et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2016; Lee and Weerts, 2016; Striepens et al., 2013) and atosiban (Lamont and Kam, 2008; Lundin et al., 1986) have been shown to be bioavailable when administered intranasally.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fresh oxytocin and atosiban solutions were made every 3 days during the period of data collection.
source: Fresh oxytocin and atosiban solutions were made every 3 days during the period of data collection, such that for each participant in the drug administration experiments, the solution he received was prepared in less than 3 days before.
evidence: This describes the drug preparation procedure.

claim: The prepared drug solutions were stored in 10 ml sterilized nasal spray bottles at 4°C until usage.
source: The prepared solutions were stored in 10 ml sterilized nasal spray bottles at 4°C until usage.
evidence: This describes the drug storage procedure.

claim: Difference limen is an index of temporal discrimination sensitivity.
source: and half the interquartile range of the fitted function corresponds to difference limen, an index of temporal discrimination sensitivity.
evidence: This defines the difference limen measure used in the analysis.
